articles.title: Dual kinase inhibition provides early clues to restoration of neuroimmune homeostasis in an AAV-haSyn model of Parkinsons disease
articles.content: Background Previous studies of drugs targeting mixed linage kinase type 3 (MLK3) and/or leucine rich repeat kinase type 2 (LRRK2) in sporadic Parkinsons disease (PD) have failed to meet clinical endpoints despite multiple lines of evidence implicating these kinases in pathogenesis. This has reduced enthusiasm for MLK3 and LRRK2 as druggable targets. Largely overlooked is the evidence that these targets remain valid but must be considered in combination to achieve a therapeutic outcome. This provides the rationale for this study. Methods We conducted a pilot study modeling early, pre-symptomatic PD with subsequent evaluation of therapeutic potential of a multi-kinase inhibitor (URMC-099) in alleviating disease pathology. Sprague Dawley rats received unilateral intranigral injections of low dose AAV-haSyn. After a two-week recovery period, all animals were administered either once-daily intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of URMC-099 or its vehicle control until their terminal endpoint. Induction of early PD, and its alleviation with URMC-099, was evaluated by lateralized motor impairment using the cylinder test and immunohistochemical analysis of neuropathology in the substantia nigra (SN) and striatum. Finally, an in vitro microglial PD model exposed to aSyn pre-formed fibrils and treated with URMC-099 was used to further evaluate the mechanism underlying therapeutic activity. Results A unilateral model of early and progressive AAV-haSyn model for PD was used to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of a targeted multi-kinase inhibitor to attenuate PD-associated neuropathology and prevent the manifestation of lateral motor deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed protection of neuronal cellular integrity along the nigral-striatal pathway with once-daily i.p. URMC-099. The mitigation of degenerative neuropathology was linked to targeted inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2 and complemented by reduced levels of gliosis in astrocytes and microglia in the SN. Single-microglia segmentation analysis suggested URMC-099 treatment preserved dynamic effector state switching in microglia to enhance autophagic flux to reduce the overall burden of pathologic aSyn. Transcriptomic analysis of a complementary in vitro microglia model corroborated the retention of a homeostatic-like effector state with URMC-099 treatment that was unique to MLK3/LRRK2 dual inhibition. Conclusions Unilateral injection of low dose AAV-haSyn successfully resulted in a lateralized model of early, progressive PD. Dual inhibition of aberrant MLK3 and LRRK2 activity with once-daily i.p. URMC-099 therapy significantly mitigated the development of PD pathology and progression in an early manifest phenotype. Our results present a potential mechanism of therapeutic action dependent on the dual inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2. This presents a novel therapeutic modality that may be beneficial to a broad population of etiologic PD patients.

articles.title: Shikonin alleviates bone cancer pain through suppression of spinal IGF2-associated p38 MAPK signaling
articles.content: Background Bone cancer pain (BCP) is a debilitating complication of advanced cancer that substantially impairs physical function and emotional wellbeing. Current pharmacological treatments often provide incomplete analgesia and may be limited by adverse effects. Shikonin, a bioactive naphthoquinone derived from Lithospermum erythrorhizon, exhibits analgesic and anti inflammatory activities, but its effects and underlying mechanisms in BCP remain unclear. Methods A rat model of BCP was established by intratibial inoculation of luciferase labeled MADB106 cells. The analgesic and behavioral effects of intrathecal Shikonin were evaluated using mechanical and thermal nociceptive assays, CatWalk gait analysis, the open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), light/dark box (LDB) test, and rotarod testing. Bioluminescence imaging and hematoxylin eosin staining were used to characterize tumor development and bone pathology. Spinal dorsal horn transcriptomic sequencing was performed to identify candidate molecular pathways. Western blotting, quantitative PCR, and ELISA were used to examine IGF2 associated p38 MAPK signaling and proinflammatory cytokines. The functional involvement of IGF2 and p38 associated signaling was further evaluated using intrathecal IGF2 siRNA and the p38 inhibitor Adezmapimod (SB203580). Results Intrathecal Shikonin produced dose and time dependent antinociceptive effects in BCP rats, with an estimated ED50 of 29.80 g/kg, and did not produce an apparent impairment of rotarod performance. Shikonin also improved gait abnormalities and pain related anxiety like behaviors. Transcriptomic analysis identified Igf2 as a candidate gene responsive to Shikonin treatment, and spinal IGF2 and p38 phosphorylation were increased during BCP development. Shikonin significantly reduced IGF2 expression and p38 phosphorylation in the spinal dorsal horn, accompanied by decreased IL 6, IL 1{beta};, and TNF ; expression in spinal tissue. IGF2 knockdown reproduced the analgesic and behavioral effects of Shikonin and reduced p38 phosphorylation, whereas p38 inhibition reproduced key behavioral effects without a marked change in IGF2 expression. Combined treatment with Shikonin and either IGF2 knockdown or p38 inhibition produced no significant additional behavioral benefit. Conclusion Intrathecal Shikonin alleviates nociceptive hypersensitivity, functional impairment, and pain related anxiety like behaviors in rats with MADB106 induced BCP. The phenocopying and non additive effects of IGF2 knockdown and p38 inhibition support the involvement of an IGF2 associated p38 MAPK signaling axis in the analgesic actions of Shikonin.

articles.title: BVLab-analyzer: a unified visual toolbox for terabyte-scale whole-brain cell detection, neuron reconstruction, and vascular network extraction
articles.content: BVLab-Analyzer is a standalone graphical software tool for end-to-end analysis of terabyte-scale whole-brain microscopy images. Operating through a zero-code interface, it handles data import (TIFF, BioImageVision, OME-Zarr), deep learning-based semantic segmentation, 3D skeleton reconstruction, and morphological statistical analysis within a unified pipeline. The software supports three target structures—cells, neurons and vasculature—and exports their morphological reconstructions in standard SWC format. To accelerate training data preparation, Smart Annotation tools provide sub-volume interference isolation, coarse-vessel ray tracing, and skeleton auto-interpolation. For inference, optimized block-wise strategies enable a standard 3D U-Net to predict whole-brain volumes up to 12 TB on a single consumer-grade GPU, while an interrupt-and-resume engine ensures fault tolerance during extended computations. By integrating these features, BVLab-Analyzer lowers the hardware barrier for whole-brain analysis and unifies previously fragmented toolchains—from annotation and segmentation to reconstruction and quantification—into a single, accessible software environment.
articles.author: Tingwei Quan

articles.title: Natural language processing for suicidal behavior detection in short Spanish clinical notes from first-contact interviews
articles.content: IntroductionSuicide is a multifactorial phenomenon influenced by social, cultural, biological, and psychological factors, whose early detection remains challenging. According to the World Health Organization, suicide is the third leading cause of death among individuals aged 15–29 years, representing a major public health concern for young populations worldwide. In first-contact clinical settings, screening opportunities are often constrained by limited time, sparse patient information, and operational workflows. This study evaluates the feasibility of detecting suicidal behavior from short Spanish-language texts collected during initial screening interviews.MethodsThe dataset comprises 374 anonymized records labeled as “no suicidal behavior,” “ideation,” “planning,” or “attempt,” with a strong imbalance toward “attempt,” reflecting operational clinical usage rather than population-representative sampling. To address data scarcity, we applied data augmentation methods (Easy Data Augmentation for Spanish, backtranslation, and large language model-based synthesis), validated through statistical analysis and clinician-based plausibility assessments.ResultsExploratory analyses revealed highly constrained and overlapping lexical patterns across classes, indicating the challenging nature of the task. A Support Vector Machine achieved 0.53 macro F1 in binary classification (“suicidal behavior” vs. “no behavior”), while BETO, a Spanish BERT model, reached 0.36 macro F1 in multiclass classification. Under the same text-only conditions, human specialists achieved macro F1 scores of 0.29 and 0.15 respectively; however, these results were based on only 20 real texts evaluated with double annotation across five specialists and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.DiscussionAlthough performance is modest compared to studies using full clinical records, these findings suggest that short-text machine learning could support nonspecialists in first-contact settings. Future work should expand datasets and explore multimodal approaches, including voice and text, to improve clinical applicability and early detection.
articles.author: Ansel Y. Rodríguez-González

articles.title: Transformers for fMRI analysis: from spatiotemporal modeling to brain foundation models
articles.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) serves as a pivotal tool for investigating the functional organization and dynamic connectivity of the human brain, indirectly reflecting neural activity through blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. However, the high-dimensional spatiotemporal structure, prominent noise interference, and inter-individual variability of fMRI data pose significant challenges for traditional modeling methods in characterizing complex brain functional patterns. In recent years, the Transformer architecture has gained significant traction in fMRI data analysis, leveraging its self-attention mechanism to model global dependencies. It has demonstrated superior performance in tasks such as brain disease classification, functional connectivity modeling, and brain representation learning. Compared to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, Transformers can more effectively capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies and offer stronger structural scalability and cross-task transfer potential. To systematically map the development of this field, this paper proposes a unified taxonomy for Transformer-fMRI methods based on modeling dimensions. It categorizes existing research into four primary paradigms: temporal modeling, spatial modeling, spatiotemporal joint modeling, and self-supervised learning, providing a comparative analysis of their structural characteristics and applicable scenarios. Furthermore, this paper summarizes the key challenges regarding computational complexity, data dependency, and interpretability, while exploring the integration of neuroscientific priors with large-scale pre-trained models. Finally, we discuss future directions for Transformers in the construction of brain foundation models and their clinical utility.
